subsection: 3. The Irish countryside, economic crisis and the Great Famine: causes, course and government responses, 1815–1850

notes.h: Background: the Union, the French Wars and the Poor Law
notes.b: To understand the Famine you need four starting facts: who governed Ireland, who owned the land, what the war had done to farming, and what relief system already existed in 1845.
points: The Act of Union, in force from 1 January 1801, made Ireland part of the United Kingdom, so it was governed from Westminster and Dublin Castle rather than by its own parliament.
Catholics were the great majority of the population, but most landlords were Protestant, members of the Church of Ireland. This is why land disputes also had a religious and political edge.
The French Wars (which ended in 1815) had raised demand and prices for Irish grain and cattle, so farming and rents boomed. This made the later fall in prices after 1815 all the more damaging.

The 1838 Poor Law created workhouses and unions (groups of parishes) run by boards of guardians and paid for by local rates (a local property tax). About 130 unions were set up at first. There is more on this in the notes on O'Connell after 1829 and the Poor Law.
notes.tip: Keep the dates and the sequence straight: Union 1801, end of the French Wars 1815, Poor Law 1838, blight 1845.

notes.h: The Irish countryside in 1815: who held the land
notes.b: Land was the basis of wealth and power, and rural society was a ladder running from a small, mainly Protestant landlord class down to millions of landless labourers. This system is called landlordism: a few owners letting land to tenants who had little security.
points: A small class of landlords, mostly Protestant, owned nearly all the land, and many held estates in more than one county.
Absentee landlords lived in England or Dublin and ran their estates through agents, so rents left the locality and improvements were rare.
Middlemen leased large farms from landlords on long leases and sublet them in smaller lots at higher rents. Landlords increasingly ended such leases after 1815.
Strong farmers held about 30 acres or more, employed labour and often grazed cattle. They were the most secure and prosperous tenants.
Smallholders held about 5 to 30 acres, mostly as tenants-at-will (tenants with no lease), so they could be evicted at short notice.
Cottiers rented a cabin and a potato patch, paying their rent mainly in labour for the farmer or landlord rather than in money.
Landless labourers hired conacre, a patch of manured ground taken for one season to grow potatoes, often at very high rents.
Most tenants had no legal security of tenure (the right to stay on the land), and any improvement they made to their holding belonged to the landlord. This discouraged investment.
notes.tip: Do not mix up cottiers and conacre: a cottier held a cabin and patch and paid in labour, while conacre was one-season land taken by a landless labourer. Examiners link absentees, insecurity and debt to the Famine.

notes.b: Ireland's population grew fast on the back of one crop. A huge number of poor families lived on tiny plots, and that left them dangerously exposed if the potato failed.
points: Ireland's population rose from about 5 million around 1800 to about 8.2 million at the 1841 census.
Early marriage and large families were common among the poor, because a couple needed only a potato patch and a cabin to set up home.
Holdings were subdivided among sons, so by 1841 there were a very large number of tiny holdings, each too small to support a family on anything but potatoes.
The potato yielded more food per acre than any grain and grew on poor soil. Eaten with buttermilk, it gave a nutritious diet.
By the 1840s about 3 million people depended almost wholly on the potato, and a labourer ate several pounds of it a day.
The heavy-cropping but poor-quality lumper variety had spread widely among the poor. Potatoes could not be stored from one season to the next, so a failed harvest left nothing to fall back on.
The 1841 census classed about two in five houses as fourth-class: one-roomed mud cabins, the lowest category of housing.
notes.tip: For essays on social and economic change, link each cause (population growth, subdivision, potato dependence) to the vulnerability before 1845.

notes.b: After the French Wars the Irish rural economy slid into depression, a long slump of falling prices, declining rural industry and harvest failures. Landlords and tenants alike were squeezed, and the poor had few ways out.
points: Wartime demand had pushed up grain prices and rents. After Waterloo in 1815 prices fell steeply but rents fell slowly, so tenants fell into arrears (unpaid rent).
Many landlords, themselves heavily in debt from wartime spending and family settlements, could not afford to invest.
Landlords began clearing smallholders and middlemen to consolidate farms, especially for more profitable pasture, so tillage gave way to grazing and small tenants lost their land.

Rural industry declined outside north-east Ulster: hand spinning of linen collapsed against factory competition, and the Irish cotton industry declined after protective duties ended in 1824. Families lost the extra income that had paid the rent.
Partial famines and fever followed harvest failures in 1816–1817, 1822 and the 1830s. These warned of what dependence on the potato could mean.
Agrarian secret societies such as the Whiteboys (18th-century in origin), Rockites (early 1820s) and Ribbonmen used violence against landlords, agents and new tenants who took farms after evictions.

The Devon Commission (appointed 1843, report 1845), a royal commission whose members were mostly landlords, was chaired by the Earl of Devon. It found insecurity of tenure, no compensation for improvements and great poverty, but no reform followed.
Seasonal migration to Britain for the harvest, and emigration of about a million people between 1815 and 1845, were the poor's main escape routes.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about landlords' fortunes: absentees, debt, clearances and, later, evictions after 1847. Remember the Devon Commission came before the blight, and its findings led to no reform.

notes.b: The blight struck a people with no other food, and it came back year after year. The worst crop failure was in 1846, but deaths were highest in 1847, so keep the two years apart.
points: Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like organism probably carried from North America, rotted potatoes in the ground and in storage. It was first reported in Ireland in September 1845.
1845: between a third and a half of the crop was lost, causing severe hardship but few deaths in the first winter.
1846: the blight destroyed almost the entire crop, and a severe winter, the worst in memory, followed in 1846–1847.
1847 (Black '47): deaths peaked in the first half of the year. The small crop that year was healthy, but so few seed potatoes had been planted that hunger continued.
1848: the blight returned and the crop failed again. 1849 brought further failure in parts of the west and a cholera epidemic.

Most victims died of disease rather than starvation, because hungry, weakened people could not resist illness. The killers were typhus and relapsing fever (both spread by lice), dysentery, scurvy and, in 1849, cholera.
Doctors, clergy, relief workers and workhouse staff died in large numbers from fever caught from the people they treated.

Regional variation: Connacht and west Munster suffered most, with Mayo, Sligo, Roscommon, Galway, Clare and west Cork worst hit. The east and north-east suffered least, though parts of Ulster also lost heavily.
About one million people died between 1846 and 1851, and over a million emigrated. The population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851.
notes.tip: Black '47 (worst year for deaths) is not the same as 1846 (worst crop failure). Strong answers explain why the Famine lasted: repeated blight, potato dependence, poor tenant security, the seed shortage in 1847 and the withdrawal of relief.

notes.b: The first season of blight was met with the most active government response of the Famine. Peel's Conservative government tried to keep food prices down and give the poor work.
points: Peel's government secretly bought about £100,000 of Indian corn (maize) in the United States through Baring Brothers in late 1845. Secrecy avoided a rise in prices before the purchase.
The maize was sold at cost through government depots to keep prices down. It was hard to grind and caused stomach pain if badly cooked, and its yellow colour gave it the nickname Peel's brimstone.
A Relief Commission, set up in November 1845 and chaired by Sir Randolph Routh, an army commissariat officer, coordinated local relief committees, which raised subscriptions and bought food.
The Board of Works ran public works such as road building to give the poor wages to buy food, with the costs falling largely on local taxes.

Peel used the crisis to repeal the Corn Laws in June 1846. This lowered grain prices in the long run but did little for Ireland immediately, and his party split and he resigned at the end of June 1846.
Mortality in the first season was low, so Peel's measures were later judged the most effective of the Famine, although the failure of 1845 was only partial.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Peel's maize (1845–46, sold at cost) with the later Whig depots (sold at market prices, west only). Peel is a good example of effective response in a Higher essay.

notes.h: Russell's Whig government, laissez-faire and the public works, 1846–1847
notes.b: When Peel fell, a government with a very different philosophy took charge just as the blight destroyed almost the whole crop. Its faith in laissez-faire shaped everything it did.
points: Lord John Russell's Whig government took office at the end of June 1846, committed to laissez-faire: the belief that government should not interfere with trade or the food market.
It refused to import food or control prices in most of Ireland, leaving supply to private merchants. Government depots opened only in the west and sold at market prices, so the poor still had to pay.
The Labouchere Act (August 1846) relaunched the public works, with the whole cost to be repaid from local taxes. Wages were set below local rates so as not to compete with private employers.

Numbers on the works rose to about 700,000 by March 1847. Payment was by task work (a set wage for a set amount of work), often late, and weakened, poorly clad people worked in the hard winter of 1846–1847.
Wages could not keep pace with food prices, which rose sharply, and the works produced many roads that led nowhere.
Faced with rising deaths and costs, the government closed the works from March 1847 and switched to direct feeding.
notes.tip: Keep the acts apart: Labouchere Act (public works, August 1846), Temporary Relief Act (soup kitchens, February 1847), Poor Law Extension Act (June 1847). Examiners reward naming each with its date and giving reasons why the works failed.

notes.h: Soup kitchens, the Poor Law Extension Act and the end of relief, 1847–1850
notes.b: After the works failed, the government fed people directly for a few months, then handed the burden to the Poor Law. From 1847 the unions (groups of parishes running workhouses), paid for by local rates, were the only relief, and the poorest areas were the least able to pay.
points: The Temporary Relief Act (the Soup Kitchen Act, February 1847) set up government soup kitchens run by local committees, giving free rations to the destitute.

By July 1847 about three million people a day received rations. This was the most effective and cheapest relief of the Famine, but the kitchens were closed by September 1847 so that relief would pass to the Poor Law.

The Poor Law Extension Act (June 1847) made the poor law responsible for all further relief, so that Irish property would pay for Irish poverty, and it allowed outdoor relief (help outside the workhouse) for the able-bodied.
Its Gregory clause, proposed by William Gregory, MP for Dublin, refused relief to anyone holding more than a quarter of an acre of land. Smallholders had to surrender their land to qualify.
Landlords used the clause and the rising poor rates to clear estates, since they paid the rates on smaller holdings. Evictions rose sharply from 1847.
Many western unions went bankrupt because their ratepayers were ruined. Workhouses, holding far more people than they were built for, became centres of fever.

The Rate-in-Aid Act (1849) imposed a national rate of 6d in the pound on every union to support the bankrupt western unions. Ulster guardians protested that the north was paying for the south and west.
By 1850 the government treated the crisis as largely over, although local distress and high mortality continued in the west, in some places after 1850.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Gregory clause (quarter-acre, 1847) with the rate-in-aid (1849). Link the Poor Law burden and the Gregory clause to evictions when you weigh the Whig response.

notes.b: Trevelyan was the civil servant who ran the government's Famine relief, which is why his name is so closely tied to it. Historians still argue over how far he made policy and how far he only carried it out.
points: Born in Taunton, Somerset, in 1807, Trevelyan served in the East India Company in Bengal before becoming Assistant Secretary to the Treasury, its senior permanent official, in 1840.
He ran the Treasury's Famine relief from 1845, controlling the purchase of Peel's maize, the public works, the food depots and the soup kitchens.
Participant: he was the civil servant most responsible for carrying out the Whig policy of 1846–1847. Ministers such as Russell and Charles Wood, Chancellor of the Exchequer, set its principles.
He was an evangelical Protestant and a firm believer in laissez-faire and political economy. He feared that generous relief would make the Irish dependent.

He saw the Famine, as he is reported to have put it, as an act of Providence (God's will) that would force changes in the Irish land system and population, and he blamed Irish landlords and the moral character of the people.

He insisted that relief costs fall on Irish property and closed the soup kitchens in 1847. He and ministers then treated the crisis as over, though distress continued. His article and book The Irish Crisis (1848) defended the policy.
Contemporaries: the government knighted him in 1848 for his work. Irish nationalists, many relief workers and some officials in Ireland condemned his rigidity.
Later career: co-author of the Northcote–Trevelyan Report (1854) that created a merit-based civil service, and Governor of Madras from 1859. He died in 1886.

Historians: Cecil Woodham-Smith's The Great Hunger (1962) made him the villain of the Famine. Robin Haines, in Charles Trevelyan and the Great Irish Famine (2004), argued he was a scapegoat for ministers and worked hard within his orders. Most see his ideology as typical of the Whig government.
notes.tip: State his post and dates, what he controlled (maize, works, depots, soup kitchens) and his beliefs, and separate the civil servant from the ministers who set policy (Russell, Wood).

notes.h: Assessment: how effective were government responses?
notes.b: Judging the responses means weighing real successes against serious failures, and weighing the views of people at the time against those of later historians. A strong answer states a judgement and keeps it up with paired points.
points: Strength: Peel's maize, relief committees and public works kept deaths low in 1845–1846.
Strength: the 1847 soup kitchens showed that direct feeding could reach about three million people a day cheaply.
Weakness: the Whigs' faith in laissez-faire meant no control of food prices, and the public works paid too little, too late, to people too weak to work.
Weakness: the decision that Irish property must pay, through the Poor Law from 1847, put the burden on the poorest unions just when they were bankrupt.
Weakness: the Gregory clause turned relief into a tool for clearance, and relief was withdrawn in 1847 while hunger continued.

Food exports: grain, cattle, pigs and butter continued to leave Irish ports. Some historians note that imports, mainly of maize, later exceeded grain exports, so the debate is over what the government could have done with the food.

Contemporary view: John Mitchel, writing in 1861, said, "The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine." This nationalist view made the Famine a central grievance against the Union.

Later view: historians such as Cormac Ó Gráda and Christine Kinealy agree the scale of death was not inevitable and that a richer United Kingdom could have spent far more. Most reject the charge of deliberate genocide but blame ideology, parsimony (meanness with money) and indifference.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay on effectiveness rewards a stated judgement, paired points (Peel's maize and committees against Whig laissez-faire, low-paid works, closed soup kitchens, the Poor Law burden and the Gregory clause), named acts with dates, numbers given with about, and Mitchel weighed against later historians.

keyTerms.definition: The system in which a small, mainly Protestant class of landlords owned the land and let it to tenants without security of tenure, often through middlemen and agents.
The slump in Irish agriculture after 1815, when prices fell, rural industry collapsed and harvest failures left the poor more dependent on the potato.
The belief that government should not interfere with the economy or the market, which led Russell's Whig government to leave food supply to private traders during the Famine.
A catastrophic shortage of food causing mass death from hunger and disease; in Ireland, the Great Famine of 1845–1850 caused by repeated failures of the potato crop.
Land rented for one season, usually manured ground for potatoes, the main means by which landless labourers fed their families.
A rural labourer who rented a cabin and potato patch, paying the rent mostly in labour.
A tenant who leased land from the landlord on a long lease and sublet it in smaller lots at a profit.
The quarter-acre clause of the Poor Law Extension Act 1847, which denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre of land.
A national poor rate of 6d in the pound imposed on every union in 1849 to support the bankrupt western unions.
Government-funded relief schemes such as road building, which gave the poor wages to buy food in 1846–1847.

factCards.term: Charles Trevelyan: three roles in the Famine
factCards.definition: As Assistant Secretary to the Treasury he ran the public works, the food depots and the soup kitchens, and he defended limited relief in The Irish Crisis (1848).

factCards.term: Five classes in the countryside in 1815
factCards.definition: Landlords (many absentee), middlemen, strong farmers, smallholders and cottiers, with landless labourers depending on conacre.
A royal commission chaired by the Earl of Devon that found insecurity of tenure, no compensation for improvements and great poverty.
1845: a third to a half lost; 1846: almost all lost; 1847: healthy but very small; 1848: lost again.
The year 1847, when Famine deaths peaked, especially in the first half of the year, from hunger and fever.
Typhus and relapsing fever, dysentery, scurvy and, in 1849, cholera killed more people than starvation itself.
About £100,000 of American maize sold at cost, a Relief Commission and local committees, and public works under the Board of Works.
Under the Labouchere Act costs fell on local taxes and wages were low; about 700,000 were employed by March 1847 before the works closed.
The Temporary Relief Act of February 1847 set up free soup kitchens that fed about three million people a day by July 1847.
It made the poor law responsible for all relief, allowed outdoor relief and included the Gregory (quarter-acre) clause.
About one million died and over a million emigrated; the population fell from about 8.2 million to about 6.6 million.

factCards.definition: Connacht and west Munster, especially Mayo, Sligo, Roscommon, Galway, Clare and west Cork; the east and north-east suffered least.
